card.title: Settle a conflict
card.blurb: Two branches changed `cat.txt`, so the merge stopped. Finish it by marking the file settled and committing - then call one off and leave no trace.
hero.eyebrow: Git · Part three · Bringing work back
hero.title: Settle a conflict
intro.0: A stopped merge feels like a hole you have fallen into, so the instinct is to close the terminal and hope it goes away. That is how half-finished merges end up committed by accident. There are only two ways out of one, and both are short: finish it by saying which file is settled, or call the whole thing off and stand exactly where you were before. Here you do both, on the same pair of branches.
meta.label: Bringing work back · Settle a conflict
concept.gt-abort.def: Calling a stopped merge off and going back to how things were before you started it.
task.1.title: Finish the stopped merge
task.1.context:
Both branches rewrote the same line of `cat.txt`, so `git merge fix` stops and saves nothing. Git will not choose between them for you.

It writes both versions into the file, wrapped in markers, with the original line between them so you can see what it was. Your job is to leave the text you want and delete the rest. Then `git add cat.txt` says that file is settled, and `git commit` writes the merge commit that was waiting on you.
task.1.goal.0: Standing on `main`, run `git merge fix` and read what it prints.
task.1.goal.1: Read `cat.txt` in the panel, then keep the line you want and drop the markers: `echo -e "Mia, tabby, 4 years old.\nSleeps on the keyboard.\nFed at seven." > cat.txt`.
task.1.goal.2: Say it is settled with `git add cat.txt`.
task.2.title: Call one off instead
task.2.context:
Same two branches, and this time the merge is already stopped - `git status` will show `cat.txt` unmerged.

You do not have to finish it. `git merge --abort` puts everything back to how it was before you started. Then pin a name on the commit you are left standing on, so this spot is easy to find again.
task.2.goal.0: Check where you are with `git status`.
task.2.goal.1: Call the merge off with `git merge --abort`.
task.2.goal.2: Pin the commit you are on with `git tag before-merge`.
task.3.title: Settle a conflict - recap
task.3.context: A stopped merge is a question. You answer it, or you withdraw it.
task.3.summaryIntro: Git stops on the one thing it cannot work out alone, and until you say something it saves nothing at all. That is why a conflict is safe to sit with - the old commits are all still there while you think.
task.3.summaryItems.0.title: Conflict -
task.3.summaryItems.0.text: git stopping because both branches changed the same file, with no commit made yet.
task.3.summaryItems.1.title: `git add cat.txt` -
task.3.summaryItems.1.text: mid-merge this stages nothing; it says that file is settled and git can move on.
task.3.summaryItems.2.title: `git commit -m "merge fix"` -
task.3.summaryItems.2.text: finishes the paused merge, saving the commit with two parents.
task.3.summaryItems.3.title: `git merge --abort` -
task.3.summaryItems.3.text: calls the whole merge off and leaves you exactly where you started it.
task.3.summaryClose: Next: fixing the commit you just made, instead of piling an `oops` on top of it.
task.1.goal.3: Finish with `git commit -m "merge fix"` - it lands with two parents.
